quote: We spent longer than expected agreeing definitions, and it was the right call. Every week we deferred that was a week of people building on sand.
The thing that sold it internally was that we stopped maintaining per-customer anything. One dashboard, filtered per viewer, and the backlog disappeared.
The pastoral team stopped asking us for lists. They just look. That sounds small and it changed how the whole department works.
Half the value was the argument we had to have about what an appointment actually is. The tooling just made us finish it.
It reframed an argument we had been having for two years. Retail was not underperforming. It was absorbing the returns.
The recovered hours were the business case. Customers catching delays on the day was the actual benefit.
Nobody asked for more detail. They asked for it sooner.
We did not have anyone to spare for reporting. That was the whole point of automating it.
Being able to show the auditor the policy rather than describe it was the difference.
If we had built it ourselves it would still be in progress. And it would be worse.
Three weeks in and the finance team has stopped emailing me. I did not know that was possible.
Shipped customer-facing analytics in three weeks with five engineers. Still slightly suspicious that it was that easy.
Spent a decade building reporting features nobody wanted to maintain. Wish this had existed in 2016.
The sandboxing model is the first multi-tenant permissions design I have read and immediately understood.
Our marketing team writes their own queries now. I am not sure I have fully processed this.
Killed a weekly spreadsheet that two people had been producing by hand since 2019. Good day.
Set this up on a Thursday afternoon expecting to spend the following week on it. Did not need the week.
The drill-through is the feature I did not know I wanted and now cannot work without.
Line supervisors who had never opened a reporting tool are now the heaviest users. That was not the plan and it is better than the plan.
Open source mattered to us for reasons that were mostly about budget and turned out to be mostly about control.
I keep expecting to hit the wall where I have to drop to SQL. Three months in, I hit it twice, and both times the escape hatch was right there.
Every BI tool claims non-technical people can use it. This is the first one where I have watched it actually happen.
